title: Reading trumpeters versus improvisers
summary: He names the dependable reading trumpeters, explains legit versus improvising players and says improvising is a natural gift.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Who were the better trumpet players around that time? Huh?

Who were the better trumpet players? Well, Perez and Kimball and a fella by name of Matoyer and those old men like Old Man and Morett, and fellas like that, you know, they were about the best men you could rely on, you know, if you hired them, if you had music, you could play, you see.
Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Sight readers, yeah.

Yeah, I played with him too. He was a personal friend of mine, he was a nice fellow too. He played nice trumpet too. He was a legit trumpet, no jazz or nothing, he was straight. And there was another fellow who played nice too, Peter LaCasse. He was a legit trumpet player too.
What's the difference between a legit trumpet player and a...

Well, some men can improvise and some men play strictly about music, you see. Now you'll take some fellows, if you ain't got the parts there, they can't play, you see. They can't remember, you know. They can't commit anything to memory. And another guy will play a tune once, or play a spark once, and he don't need it the most. Well that's the difference, you see. But when you say a legit man is a man that, and if you've got music he'll play it, but he ain't going to put nothing to it, you see. He'll play it all right. But another guy will play it and then improvise on it too, you see. Build it up. Could they improvise these fellows? Well that's a gift mostly, I think. That's mostly a gift, you see. Everybody don't hear that, you know. You don't learn that. It's got to be natural, you see.
And these fellows like Twy and Black Charles, could they improvise?
Not very much. They didn't play the style we're playing now, you see. They played mostly straight, nice trumpet but straight, you know.
You could improvise? Huh? You could improvise? Oh yeah, sure.

I always could do that, you know. Well I used to play in our band. I'd play a stock two, three times, I didn't need the music anymore. I could just remember it, you understand? Sure. Just like anything else, you understand. Natural.
Do you remember any other good trumpet men around that time? No.

Particular good? Well George McCullum, he was a very nice trumpet man too. You ever read in May? Yes, very good. He taught a little Alcorn, you know, Alvin. Alvin? That's his teacher, yeah. I think they were cousins. I don't know whether they were related or not, but I know he taught him. He's very good. He played a lot in the Excelsior Band, you know.
